title: Norie Campbell & Jen Ruddick — Thomson Reuters legal department (GCO 2030)
pub: Clarity on Tech, Thomson Reuters Institute (YouTube)
author: Norie Campbell · Jen Ruddick · Lizzy Duffy · Zach Warren

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Campbell does not accept the cluster’s central framing that automation chiefly threatens junior expertise reproduction. She instead argues that AI can accelerate younger lawyers’ effectiveness and shifts the main adaptation concern toward established practitioners, while acknowledging—but not endorsing—predictions of smaller, more senior teams.
qs: I think that there's often immediate reaction to oh well, I'll have gotten rid of um basic work and therefore what I won't need is lawyers who are learning how to practice law.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Ruddick reports GC predictions of smaller, more senior, AI-native legal departments that raise a genuine junior-pipeline question, aligning with the cluster’s concern. Campbell, however, explicitly rejects juniors as the main concern, expects AI-familiar entrants to be ready if GCs provide appropriate tools, and shifts the perceived vulnerability toward newly promoted partners. These are forecasts and personal expectations, not measured workforce or training outcomes.
qs: Many of the GCs I've spoken to predict that there'll be a smaller legal team made up made up of probably more senior lawyers  more AI native lawyers.
>> So the concern I hear the most is the  one that you're saying you know what's going to happen to the junior lawyers but I have to say that's not my concern.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central augmentation thesis that AI will reshape legal work without eliminating lawyers. It materially extends the cluster by arguing that AI can accelerate junior-lawyer effectiveness and distribute departmental knowledge, while shifting adaptation pressure toward established practitioners trained under the prior paradigm.
qs: They're going to be replaced by lawyers who know how to use AI and that that fundamentally underpins my view.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central proposition that selective, human-led deployment and operating-model redesign are decisive. It materially extends that proposition with an early legal-department implementation model: define a strategy and roadmap, concentrate resources on high-impact workflows, engage diverse champions, and embed expert testing, human involvement and ongoing audits.
qs: And narrowed our focus and concentrated our efforts on select priorities and that targeted approach brought about much more meaningful transformation in the areas that we were focused on.

And I think that also means creating appropriate governance checkpoints in the AI workflows so that you're you're building things that have been tested by subject matter  experts and there's a human in the loop and there's ongoing audits of your technology.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s buyer-led, augmentation-oriented account: it treats efficiency as insufficient, anticipates potentially smaller and more senior in-house teams, and emphasizes focused implementation, workforce readiness and psychologically safe experimentation. Its staffing claims are explicitly forecasts rather than measured outcomes, consistent with the cluster’s caution about the early evidence base.
qs: And I say that because if you if you set your goal for yourself on the use of AI to do only efficiency, you really will have missed the true upside here.
Many of the GCs I've spoken to predict that there'll be a smaller legal team made up made up of probably more senior lawyers  more AI native lawyers.

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s deliberate-implementation thesis by framing AI adoption as an organisational change challenge requiring tailored planning, leadership and change management rather than a plug-and-play technology purchase. Its scope is corporate legal departments, however, so it does not provide evidence that AI expands access to civil justice or improves service outcomes.
qs: But for the GCO office of the future to succeed around AI, it will mean it's more than just a tech issue.
It will require true planning, leadership, [music] and change management to succeed.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s expectation of structural workforce change: GCs predict smaller, more senior and AI-native legal teams and explicitly question the junior pipeline. Campbell adds a caveat rather than rejecting the proposition, arguing that incoming lawyers may be AI-ready and that newly promoted partner-level lawyers may face greater risk. The evidence is predictive and buyer-side, not proof of law-firm revenue loss or profession-wide contraction.
qs: Many of the GCs I've spoken to predict that there'll be a smaller legal team made up made up of probably more senior lawyers  more AI native lawyers.
And so the question they're asking is where does that leave the very junior lawyers?

st.t: Legal leadership: Business capability complements legal expertise
st.an: The source supports the proposition that effective legal leadership extends beyond legal expertise. It emphasises people leadership and change management—especially helping lawyers operate confidently amid ambiguity—and identifies cross-functional leadership across HR, marketing and project management as relevant experience. Its claims are experience-based rather than measured outcomes.
qs: You have to put the supports around lawyers to give them the confidence that in this very ambiguous and fast-moving world they're going to be able to nail it, get the advice right, and really shine across the company.
I had the opportunity of leading a global HR group, a global marketing group, a global enterprise project management office.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s emphasis on organisational readiness and workforce adaptation: it assigns general counsel responsibility for providing AI tools and argues that lawyers’ ability to use AI will shape competitive outcomes. Its smaller-team forecast is explicitly reported as GCs’ prediction rather than demonstrated evidence, consistent with the cluster’s qualification of labour-market claims.
qs: They're going to be very ready and it's going to be up to the general counsel to be making sure that the tools that they need are available to them when they get to the workplace.
They're going to be replaced by lawyers who know how to use AI and that that fundamentally underpins my view.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s engagement-first position by treating AI adoption as an organisational process requiring active leadership, planning and change management rather than passive reliance on a plug-and-play tool. It reinforces the implementation-support point but provides neither empirical findings nor a broader public-interest or governance argument.
qs: But for the GCO office of the future to succeed around AI, it will mean it's more than just a tech issue.
It will require true planning, leadership, [music] and change management to succeed.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source directly supports treating legal AI as organisational change rather than a software purchase. It attributes progress to a focused strategy and roadmap, leadership-created space for experimentation, and links between frontline ideas and central priorities; its evidence is qualitative experience rather than quantified transformation outcomes.
qs: And I really think the true progress started when we defined an AI strategy and roadmap.
So a big part of the leadership role is creating the space where it's okay to experiment to share what's working, what's not without having to feel like you've got it all figured out.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s complementarity framing: it rejects the assumption that automating basic work necessarily removes the need for junior lawyers and instead predicts AI-enabled adaptation, faster junior development and broader knowledge sharing. Its employment confidence rests on an early-stage proposal and historical analogy rather than measured AI outcomes, consistent with the cluster’s caution about aggregate staffing effects.
qs: I think that there's often immediate reaction to oh well, I'll have gotten rid of um basic work and therefore what I won't need is lawyers who are learning how to practice law.

kp.k: GCO 2030 makes internal transformation a research subject
kp.d: The episode presents GCO 2030 as a collaboration between the Thomson Reuters Institute and the company's general counsel's office to develop a future vision and document AI-driven change from inside the department. Campbell says the Institute supplies rigor, strategic structure and feedback to support evidence-based decisions rather than anecdotes. The discussion describes an ongoing project at an early stage, rather than presenting a completed impact study.
qs: making itself the subject of its own transformation research.
you're helping us actually do this transformation evidence-based.
we're obviously at the beginning of our GCO 2030 work.

kp.k: Concentrated workflow priorities outperformed broad experimentation
kp.d: Ruddick reports that attempting to address all potentially AI-enabled workflows dispersed resources and produced incremental improvements rather than big wins. She attributes more meaningful transformation to defining an AI strategy and roadmap, narrowing priorities and concentrating effort on initiatives with the greatest potential impact. This is a qualitative account of the department's experience; no quantified productivity or financial results are supplied.
qs: Trying to kind of prove everything at once. And that led to some incremental improvements for some of our workflows, but it really didn't yield those big wins.
And narrowed our focus and concentrated our efforts on select priorities and that targeted approach brought about much more meaningful transformation in the areas that we were focused on.

kp.k: Mandatory certification established a shared AI skills baseline
kp.d: Duffy describes a mandatory certification program of what she recalls as eight modules, with 100% completion; Ruddick confirms completion and explains that the beginner program established a department-wide baseline using actual legal work. Sessions incorporated real use cases, participation and homework, with recordings available for certification and high live attendance. An advanced certificate accommodates different skill levels and interests. Positive feedback and completion are reported, not measured improvements in legal competence.
qs: I think it was eight modules. It was mandatory participation. You you reached 100% completion.
It's about creating that baseline for the whole department.
So we had homework, we had, you know, type in on the session itself. And like you said, 100% completion and really a ton of positive feedback after it.

kp.k: Champions connect grassroots experimentation with central strategy
kp.d: Ruddick describes AI champions as practitioners close to the work whose experiments generate ideas that are spotlighted across the department and fed into the central roadmap for scaling. Campbell says champions span practice groups, organizational tenure and career stages, rather than fitting a single demographic profile. Their peer stories help explain the practical value of adoption while accommodating uneven readiness across the team.
qs: They are the closest to the best ideas because they're out there doing the work.
these incredible ideas that they're coming up with are being fed back to the central AI strategy team. They can be added to our road map to be scaled in other parts of of the department.
They're new to the organization, they're new to career, they're long in their career, etc.

kp.k: Reusable workflows let adoption spread across practice areas
kp.d: Campbell recommends champion-led use cases with relevance across teams, citing NDAs used by both M&A and go-to-market lawyers. Ruddick reports discovering that apparently different subject areas share a small set of underlying workflow types, such as reviewing a contract against a playbook. She sees identifying those similarities as a way to transfer solutions and stimulate further ideas across a broadly constituted department.
qs: if you can get a use case started with a champion, but that has relevance to other teams, then that it starts to spread.
it's just a you know a review of a contract against a playbook and that's what it comes down to.
we have such broad practices but really there's there's only a handful of kind of types of workflows.

kp.k: Leadership must integrate people and technology deliberately
kp.d: Campbell uses a technology-adoption analogy from a 2018 TED Talk: an organization would invest substantial onboarding effort in a new leader paid $500,000 and should show comparable intentionality toward technology. She argues that in-house leaders now need technological understanding alongside legal expertise, business acumen and people leadership, including deciding how projects should be delivered through both people and tools. Bringing the team along is part of the leadership task, not something accomplished simply by announcing a strategy.
qs: And this was 2018. So, this was not generative AI adoption.
do you do the same thing if you introduce technology to your team that you would do if you introduced a new leader?
You need to have the ability to use technology and understand how technology does your work.
we will make the journey part of the reward, that it will be about bringing people along.

kp.k: Junior displacement is questioned, not established
kp.d: Duffy reports that many GCs she has interviewed predict smaller departments staffed by more senior, AI-native lawyers, raising concerns about junior opportunities. Campbell explicitly takes a different view: she expects AI-familiar entrants to be ready and places responsibility on GCs to provide their tools. Her greater concern is adaptation by established practitioners, exemplified by lawyers who have just made partner after learning an earlier practice paradigm. These are contrasting expectations, not observed staffing outcomes.
qs: Many of the GCs I've spoken to predict that there'll be a smaller legal team made up made up of probably more senior lawyers more AI native lawyers.
what's going to happen to the junior lawyers but I have to say that's not my concern.
the cohort that I worry about the most in the legal profession are kind of the people who in the law firm terminology just made partner
They've done all this effort into learning how to do their work one way and a new world is ahead of them.

kp.k: AI could accelerate junior effectiveness and knowledge sharing
kp.d: Campbell argues that removing basic tasks need not eliminate lawyers learning to practice: tools could accelerate younger lawyers' effectiveness and distribute a baseline understanding of the department's advice. She invokes her own first-year experience of a securities bulletin moving online, which she recalls improving briefs without eliminating junior work. This is an analogy supporting her outlook, not evidence of generative AI's employment effects. She acknowledges that efficiencies will change departments but says the eventual form remains to be demonstrated.
qs: the use of the tools can empower and enable younger lawyers to be accelerated into effectiveness
to share knowledge across the legal department so that anyone in the department has a base level understanding of the kind of advice we give on questions.
What the only impact it had was to actually make a better brief because it was easier to find the relevant um information.
that will change the uh overall complexion of uh general counsel's office. I think how is still going to be um proved out

kp.k: Capability gains should accompany efficiency goals
kp.d: Campbell regards efficiency as necessary but argues that focusing exclusively on it misses AI's larger potential to improve lawyers' proficiency and the department's ability to participate in business decisions at business speed. Her recommendation is to frame adoption around enhanced professional capabilities rather than only the reduction of work or staffing.
qs: efficiency baseline. You must get efficiency. But the game changer here is proficiency.
if you set your goal for yourself on the use of AI to do only efficiency, you really will have missed the true upside here.
how is this making a um legal department that's more ready to be sitting at the table, is more ready to act at the speed of business.

kp.k: Adaptability combines legal strengths with overcoming professional caution
kp.d: Discussing the adaptability quotient framework introduced by Duffy, Campbell argues that lawyers' rapid information processing, navigation of ambiguity, lifelong learning and ability to consider different perspectives support adaptation. Conversely, reliance on precedent, concern for correctness and trust, and comfort with established methods can discourage experimentation. She recommends leadership support that enables lawyers to adapt confidently while maintaining sound advice.
qs: lawyers by training are capable of taking in like a massive amount of information quickly.
Lawyers by nature are lifelong learners.
we have to do things the way we've done it before and that gives me comfort and confidence.

You have to put the supports around lawyers to give them the confidence that in this very ambiguous and fast-moving world they're going to be able to nail it, get the advice right, and really shine across the company.

kp.k: Using AI can inform enterprise AI risk advice
kp.d: Campbell identifies a dual opportunity for in-house lawyers: they must advise on complex substantive legal issues surrounding organizational AI adoption while also using AI tools in their own work. She argues that direct tool experience can help them understand the technology and inform enterprise risk mitigation. Her characterization of legal AI tools as among the best available is a speaker assessment, not a comparative evaluation presented in the episode.
qs: at the very same moment we're learning about the substantive legal issues around AI, we were able to have the lawyers using the tools themselves.
they have this chance both to understand it as a tool by actually using it and to help inform how to mitigate the risks of it across an organization.

kp.k: Continuous adaptation matters more than staying ahead
kp.d: Ruddick says the pace of AI development makes staying ahead of everything unrealistic. She recommends building a department able to adapt continuously, retry approaches and concentrate deeply on the areas where AI matters most. She reports experiments repeated three or four times, sometimes improving and sometimes establishing that a particular approach did not work, illustrating an iterative rather than one-time transformation process.
qs: I don't think in this moment the goal can be to stay ahead of everything.
I see the goal is kind of building a department that can adapt continuously.
Tried things, you know, three, four times and and improved every time or decided it didn't work um one way.
get very clear on where AI matters most for your department and then really go deep there.

kp.k: Safe experimentation requires governance and human oversight
kp.d: Ruddick recommends making it safe for risk-aware lawyers to learn publicly and share failures without needing to appear already proficient. She couples that permission with appropriate workflow governance checkpoints, subject-matter-expert testing, a human in the loop and ongoing technology audits to build confidence. Campbell likewise emphasizes lawyers' ability to guide tools. The recommended model retains human oversight rather than relying on autonomous output.
qs: For me it's been important to making it feel safe to learn publicly especially in a legal department.
creating the space where it's okay to experiment to share what's working, what's not without having to feel like you've got it all figured out.

creating appropriate governance checkpoints in the AI workflows so that you're you're building things that have been tested by subject matter experts and there's a human in the loop and there's ongoing audits of your technology.
they'll be able to be the human in the loop, guide the tool.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Campbell and Ruddick describe AI as a means of improving legal capability as well as efficiency, with transformation dependent on focused workflows, workforce learning and human oversight.
pts.d: Jen Ruddick reports that trying to improve all potentially AI-suitable workflows at once produced incremental gains but not major wins; concentrating resources on a defined strategy and selected priorities produced more meaningful transformation in Thomson Reuters' legal department. She also claims that apparently different practice areas share a small set of underlying workflows, allowing solutions such as contract review against a playbook to transfer across teams. Ruddick describes champions as both spreading adoption through peer examples and feeding practical ideas into the central roadmap for scaling. Norie Campbell argues that in-house leadership now requires technological competence alongside business acumen and people leadership, with legal expertise remaining foundational: leaders must allocate work across both people and technology. On careers, Campbell explicitly endorses the proposition that lawyers who use AI will replace lawyers who do not, rather than AI simply replacing lawyers. She is more concerned about established practitioners who have recently mastered the previous working paradigm than about incoming juniors. She predicts that AI can accelerate younger lawyers' effectiveness and distribute a baseline of institutional legal knowledge across a department. She acknowledges that efficiencies will change the composition of general counsel offices but leaves the eventual form unresolved. Her principal upside claim is increased proficiency and business responsiveness, not merely lower effort. Finally, Campbell argues that lawyers' direct use of AI tools can help them understand and mitigate AI-related risks across their organisations. The smaller, more senior future-team prediction relayed by the interviewer from unnamed GCs is not presented as Campbell's own forecast.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is principally internal implementation experience and illustrative anecdotes; the episode reports training completion but no measured legal-output or workforce effects.
pts.d: Ruddick bases the targeted-strategy and workflow-transfer claims on her experience implementing AI within the Thomson Reuters general counsel's office, including similar playbook-review needs arising in different business segments. She reports 100% completion of the department's training, strong live attendance and positive feedback. These are participation and reception indicators, not quantified demonstrations of productivity or legal quality. Campbell recounts a champion's report that using CoCounsel resolved a late-Friday problem that otherwise appeared likely to consume the weekend; no task specifics, time comparison or output assessment are supplied. Campbell says the embedded Thomson Reuters Institute collaboration brings research discipline and evidence-based feedback, but the episode does not present a research methodology, comparison group, benchmark results or quantified savings. Her forecasts concerning junior lawyers, adaptation and proficiency rest on leadership judgment and experience. She invokes the historical move of a securities-law bulletin online, which she recalls improving briefs without eliminating junior work, as an analogy rather than direct evidence about generative AI. Her technology-onboarding recommendation draws on a 2018 TED Talk about technology adoption generally. Both the legal department and the Institute are part of Thomson Reuters, and the account is an internal transformation narrative rather than an external evaluation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Reported adoption gains concern an ongoing, early-stage transformation in the 2026 episode; longer-term workforce and capability claims have no firm delivery dates and depend on training, adaptation and governance.
pts.d: The discussion takes place within GCO 2030, but Campbell describes the project as being at its beginning; the title is a planning horizon, not a dated commitment to a particular staffing outcome. Ruddick presents prioritisation, cross-team reuse and training as current experience, while Campbell's junior-development and departmental-capability claims are prospective. Campbell conditions new entrants' readiness on their exposure to AI during education and outside work, and on GCs supplying the tools they need. She stresses that adoption is gradual, that people start at different levels, and that not everyone will become a champion at the same pace. Ruddick argues that rapid changes in capability make continuous adaptation more realistic than staying ahead of everything: practices may change within a month, and implementations can require three or four attempts. Benefits are framed as augmentation with a human in the loop, not unsupervised substitution. Ruddick specifies subject-matter-expert testing, governance checkpoints and ongoing technology audits as conditions for confidence and experimentation. Campbell explicitly qualifies the staffing forecast by saying that the form of future efficiency-driven change remains to be established.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected group is corporate in-house legal departments, with distinct implications for leaders, incoming lawyers, established practitioners and internal business stakeholders.
pts.d: For GCs and practice leaders, AI changes leadership expectations: they must understand technology, provide tools and learning support, choose high-impact priorities and manage combined human-and-technology workflows. For department members, mandatory foundational training establishes common knowledge while advanced learning and champions support different levels of adoption. Campbell describes champions as spanning practice groups, organisational tenure and career stages, rather than belonging to one demographic cohort. For junior lawyers, her projected effect is faster development into effective contributors, rather than an asserted disappearance of junior roles. For practitioners comparable to newly made law-firm partners, she identifies a potentially difficult adjustment after substantial investment in a previous practice model; this is an adaptation concern, not a measured displacement finding. For M&A, go-to-market and other teams, reusable NDA and playbook-review workflows can spread improvements across practice boundaries. For the wider company, the claimed benefits are a legal department better able to respond at business speed and advise on organisational AI risks. The source does not establish law-firm headcount reductions, pricing changes, effects on ALSP competition or access-to-justice outcomes.
